problem.text: How many ways can a student schedule $3$ mathematics courses—algebra, geometry, and number theory—in a $6$-period day if no two mathematics courses can be taken in consecutive periods? (What courses the student takes during the other $3$ periods is of no concern here.)

steps.title: Where to start: split the job into two stages
steps.body: The rule "no two consecutive" is only about *which* periods hold math, not which course goes where. So first choose the $3$ periods for math, then decide which course goes in each. Count each stage and multiply.

your_turn.prompt: Is the set of periods $\{1, 3, 6\}$ allowed? What about $\{2, 3, 5\}$?
your_turn.answer: $\{1,3,6\}$ is allowed (no two are next to each other). $\{2,3,5\}$ is not, because $2$ and $3$ are consecutive.

steps.title: Choose the periods using gaps
steps.body: Line up the $3$ non-math periods. They leave $4$ gaps: one before, two between, and one after. Putting each math course in a different gap guarantees no two are adjacent, so we choose $3$ of the $4$ gaps, $\binom{4}{3} = 4$ ways. Careful: it is easy to find only the alternating sets $\{1,3,5\}$ and $\{2,4,6\}$ and miss the others.

your_turn.prompt: List all $4$ allowed sets of periods.

steps.title: Assign the courses
steps.body: The three courses are different, so once the periods are fixed, swapping two courses gives a new schedule. The number of ways to place $3$ different courses into $3$ chosen periods is the number of orderings of the courses.

your_turn.prompt: In how many ways can algebra, geometry and number theory fill periods $1$, $3$, $5$?

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: Each of the $4$ period sets can be filled in $6$ ways, so there are $4 \cdot 6 = 24$ schedules. The answer is **(E)** $24$.

wrong_choices.C: This comes from using only the alternating sets $\{1,3,5\}$ and $\{2,4,6\}$, giving $2 \cdot 6 = 12$. The sets $\{1,3,6\}$ and $\{1,4,6\}$ also avoid consecutive periods.
wrong_choices.D: This comes from finding only $3$ of the $4$ allowed period sets, giving $3 \cdot 6 = 18$. The gap method, $\binom{4}{3} = 4$, makes sure none is missed.

verification.verifier_notes: Passed adversarial verifier on first review.
